strengths: The paper identifies an important limitation of frame-pair VFI: independently synthesized frames can be inconsistent over long sequences. Recasting VFI as chunk-level sequence generation is relevant and potentially useful.

The skip-concatenate inference order is an intuitive, task-specific idea: independently generating a future chunk can reset autoregressive drift, while subsequently filling the intervening chunk can restore continuity.

The architecture combines several practical components coherently, including diffusion forcing, temporally dense but spatially local attention, tiled VAE processing, and multi-scale conditioning of the decoder on observed frames.

The reported results are promising. LDF-VFI obtains the best FVD in every setting in Table 1, with particularly large improvements at 16x interpolation, while remaining competitive in LPIPS. The component ablation also shows a substantial average FVD improvement from 22.67 to 17.05 when replacing causal sampling with skip-concatenate sampling.
The manuscript is generally easy to follow, and the diagrams communicate the overall architecture and sampling intuition effectively.
weaknesses: The evidence does not adequately support the central claim of stable long-horizon autoregressive generation. The only skip-concatenate ablation reports aggregate LPIPS/FVD at three interpolation factors; there is no quality-versus-time or quality-versus-number-of-chunks analysis, no measurement of boundary discontinuities, and no comparison across different reset intervals. Figure 4 merely assumes increasing causal error and constant skip-concatenate error rather than demonstrating either behavior. Consequently, the strong claim that error remains at a constant level regardless of video duration is unsupported.

The baseline coverage is too narrow for the claimed state of the art. Table 1 compares only four primarily flow-based methods and omits the diffusion VFI approaches emphasized in the related work, including LDMVFI, LBBDM, MAD-IFF, VIDIM, and EDEN. The manuscript does not provide empirical evidence that these methods cannot be evaluated under an adapted protocol. It also omits recent arbitrary-timestep alternatives discussed in the related work. This makes it difficult to distinguish gains from holistic modeling from gains due to using a large pretrained Wan2.1 video generator and substantially different training data or capacity.

The new benchmark protocol is underspecified. The paper does not state the number of sequences, sequence lengths, precise frame-selection procedure, resolution distribution, or FVD implementation/statistics for the main evaluations. These details are especially important because FVD can be unstable for small evaluation sets. The protocol also gives LDF-VFI access to the full sparse sequence while pairwise baselines use adjacent frames, which tests the proposed setting but does not isolate architecture quality; a matched multi-frame or oracle-context baseline is needed.

The scalability claims are stronger than the evidence. No runtime, throughput, peak-memory, FLOP, parameter-count, or resolution-scaling results are reported, and there is no ablation of sparse attention or tiled encoding. The statement that computation is decoupled from image resolution is technically inaccurate: local attention can change quadratic spatial scaling to approximately linear scaling, but token count and total computation still grow with resolution. The reported 4K inference also requires two 80 GB GPUs, without comparison to full attention or other methods.

The method is not specified sufficiently for reproduction. Important details are missing, including the spatial attention window and connectivity, DiT/model size, number of chunks in the conditioning window, exact skip-concatenate schedule for arbitrary sequence lengths, boundary handling, classifier-free or conditioning settings, tiling behavior inside the DiT, and benchmark-generation/evaluation scripts. The manuscript says code is available but provides no usable link in the submitted document.

The ablations confound components. Table 2 separately tests the sampling order only with the unconditional decoder, but adding the conditional decoder is evaluated only on top of skip-concatenate; there is no causal-plus-conditional configuration and hence no full factorial comparison or interaction analysis. There are also no ablations for holistic multi-chunk modeling, temporal context length, diffusion forcing, sparse attention, tiling, or pretrained initialization.

The conditional VAE is evaluated mainly through final task metrics, while Table 3 measures only observed-keyframe reconstruction for nearest-neighbor versus zero padding. This does not establish its effect on interpolated-frame fidelity, temporal coherence, or hallucination. Standard distortion metrics and a human preference study would strengthen the perceptual-quality claims.

Originality is moderate rather than compellingly established: diffusion forcing, tiled VAE encoding, local attention, nearest-neighbor conditioning, and ControlNet-style decoder features are established techniques. The principal new element is the skip-concatenate generation order, but it is described informally and lacks the targeted long-horizon validation necessary to establish a substantive advance.

There are several presentation issues—such as malformed equations/text extraction, grammatical errors, an imprecise output-length definition sT rather than the usual endpoint-aware interpolation length, and inconsistent naming of XTest-entire versus XTest-4K. These are correctable, but they further reduce clarity. Overall, the promising idea and FVD results are outweighed by missing comparisons, insufficient validation of the defining long-term-stability claim, and limited reproducibility.

strengths: The paper targets an important limitation of frame-pair VFI: independently generated frames can lack sequence-level coherence. Chunkwise autoregressive interpolation is a potentially useful direction, especially for long videos and high interpolation factors.

The skip-concatenate strategy is an intuitive and seemingly effective heuristic. In Table 2, replacing causal sampling with skip-concatenate reduces average FVD from 22.67 to 17.05 while retaining similar LPIPS.

The reported FVD results are strong across all four settings in Table 1. The conditional decoder also improves average LPIPS from 0.060 to 0.051 relative to the corresponding unconditional skip-concatenate configuration.

The system combines diffusion forcing, spatially local and temporally dense attention, tiled VAE processing, and input-conditioned decoding into a coherent overall architecture. The manuscript is generally understandable and includes useful component-level ablations.
weaknesses: The evaluation is insufficient to support the central claims. The paper claims arbitrary-length generation and constant long-term error, but provides no performance-versus-duration or performance-versus-chunk-index analysis. Table 2 reports aggregate FVD only, so it does not demonstrate that drift remains bounded or that skip-concatenate resets accumulated error over genuinely long sequences.

The state-of-the-art comparison is incomplete and selectively restricted to four primarily flow-based baselines. Numerous closely related methods discussed in the paper—including EDEN, LDMVFI, VIDIM, LBBDM, MAD-IF, SGM-VFI, and VFIMamba—are omitted. This substantially weakens the claimed superiority of the diffusion-based approach.

The new benchmark protocol is under-specified. The manuscript does not clearly report test-set sizes, sequence lengths, preprocessing, output-frame counts, or the precise FVD computation protocol. FVD can be unstable for small sample sets, yet no uncertainty, repeated evaluation, or complementary temporal metric is given. Single-frame qualitative snapshots also cannot establish temporal consistency.

There are serious inconsistencies between the text and results. Section 4.3 claims results on SNU-FILM-hard, SNU-FILM-extreme, and XTest-4K, whereas Table 1 reports SNU-FILM-entire at 4x/8x/16x and XTest-entire at 16x. The asserted 4K result is absent. Likewise, the abstract contains an unfinished source-code statement with no URL.

The claimed resolution scalability is not adequately demonstrated. There are no 4K quality results, memory measurements, runtimes, FLOPs, or comparisons with baselines. Moreover, local attention and tiled processing make cost roughly linear rather than independent of spatial resolution, contradicting the statement that computation is decoupled from resolution. Requiring two 80GB GPUs further calls for a careful efficiency analysis.

The flow-matching exposition is technically inconsistent: with x_t=(1-t)x_1+t x_0 and x_1 defined as noise, noise occurs at t=0 and data at t=1, but the paper says inference starts from x_1 at t=1 and integrates to t=0. This reverses the stated path and velocity direction.

Core implementation details needed for reproduction are missing, including model scale and parameter count, patch and attention-window specifications, exact receptive-field schedule, diffusion-forcing noise distribution, precise skip-concatenate generation algorithm and context layout, and boundary handling. The unavailable code compounds this problem.

Important ablations are absent. There is no direct comparison between holistic/chunkwise modeling and an otherwise matched pairwise model, no chunk-length study, no local-versus-full attention study, and no evaluation of tiled encoding artifacts. Table 3 measures only observed-keyframe VAE reconstruction and therefore does not establish that nearest-neighbor filling improves interpolation.

The comparison grants the proposed model access to the entire low-frame-rate video while baselines are run independently on adjacent pairs. Although this illustrates the proposed setting, it does not disentangle architectural gains from access to additional temporal context. A matched long-context baseline or controlled context ablation is necessary.

Overall, the idea has merit and the reported FVD improvements are promising, but consequential gaps in validation, baseline coverage, technical consistency, and reproducibility prevent the manuscript from presently supporting its broad claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important VFI limitation: independently interpolating frame pairs can produce inconsistent long sequences. Modeling several frames jointly and connecting chunks autoregressively is a well-motivated direction with clear computer-vision relevance.

The skip-concatenate schedule is simple and potentially useful. Table 2 provides supporting evidence: relative to causal sampling with the same unconditional VAE, it reduces average FVD from 22.67 to 17.05 while slightly improving LPIPS.

The conditional VAE is sensibly designed to restore details from observed frames. Its ablation yields a substantial average LPIPS improvement from 0.060 to 0.051, and Table 3 supports nearest-neighbor conditioning over zero padding.

Results in Table 1 are promising: LDF-VFI obtains the best reported FVD in every evaluated setting, with particularly large gains at 16× interpolation, while remaining competitive in LPIPS. Figure 5 also shows plausible qualitative improvements on difficult motion.

The combination of spatial tiling, local spatial attention, dense temporal attention, and chunkwise processing is practically motivated and offers a plausible path toward long and high-resolution inference.
The manuscript is generally easy to follow, with helpful architecture and sampling diagrams and reasonably complete training hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The experiments do not directly establish the central claim of bounded error or temporal stability over arbitrary-length videos. There is no quality-versus-duration analysis, chunk-boundary metric, comparison across numbers of autoregressive steps, or visualization spanning many chunks. Aggregate FVD alone cannot demonstrate that error remains at a constant level regardless of video duration.

The claimed 4K and arbitrary-resolution scalability is insufficiently supported. No 4K quantitative or qualitative result, runtime, peak-memory measurement, scaling curve, or comparison with full attention is reported. Stating that two 80GB GPUs suffice does not validate quality, efficiency, or seamless generalization.

The baseline study is narrow relative to the paper's motivation and related work. It excludes the cited diffusion-based VFI methods and strong recent approaches such as EDEN, VIDIM, LD-MVFI, SGM-VFI, and VFIMamba. Consequently, the broad state-of-the-art claim is not firmly established. LDF-VFI also trails BiM-VFI in LPIPS on SNU-FILM-16× and XTest-16×.

The newly constructed benchmarks are under-specified: the manuscript does not clearly report the number and lengths of evaluated videos, source-sequence selection, exact downsampling procedure, boundary handling, or FVD computation protocol. Because FVD can be statistically unstable on small sets and diffusion inference is stochastic, confidence intervals or results over multiple seeds are needed.

Several architectural and inference details required for reproduction are missing, including model size, precise sparse-attention window and shifting pattern, autoregressive context size, exact skip/concatenate chunk schedule, overlap or boundary handling, and a formal sampling algorithm. The manuscript says code is available but provides no usable link in the submitted text.

There is a mathematical inconsistency in Section 3.1: with x_t=(1-t)x_1+t x_0, noise x_1 occurs at t=0 and data x_0 at t=1, yet inference is described as starting from x_1 and integrating from t=1 to 0. This appears readily correctable but should be resolved for technical clarity.

The ablation does not isolate several key choices, including holistic multi-frame modeling versus independent prediction, diffusion forcing versus standard training, local versus full attention, tiled encoding, or temporal non-overlap. Thus, the evidence attributes gains to two components but not to much of the claimed overall design.

There are presentation inconsistencies that are not decision-critical but should be fixed: Section 4.3 refers to SNU-FILM hard/extreme and XTest-4K although Table 1 reports SNU-FILM-entire and XTest-entire; Figure 5 is alternately described as SNU-FILM and SNU-FILM-extreme; and the prose contains numerous grammatical and typographical errors.

strengths: The video-centric formulation addresses a real limitation of pairwise VFI: independently generated frames can be individually plausible yet temporally inconsistent. Joint chunk generation with autoregressive cross-chunk conditioning is a sensible direction.
The system combines diffusion forcing, spatially local/temporally dense attention, tiled VAE processing, and conditional decoding into a coherent pipeline that demonstrably handles 4K inputs.

The quantitative results contain meaningful positives. LDF-VFI obtains the best reported FVD in every evaluated setting, including 26.26 on SNU-FILM-16x versus 38.26 for the next-best baseline and 51.41 on X4K-16x versus 69.83. The skip-concatenate ablation reduces average FVD from 22.67 to 17.05, while conditional decoding improves average LPIPS from 0.060 to 0.051.

weaknesses: The central claim—stable generation for arbitrarily long videos with error accumulation bounded at a constant level—is not adequately established. There is no analysis of quality or boundary error as sequence length and autoregressive chunk count increase, no comparison of causal and skip-concatenate sampling over long horizons, and no theoretical argument for the claimed bound. Figure 6 shows only one small qualitative/temporal trace, while Table 3 aggregates entire sequences and therefore cannot demonstrate that drift remains bounded.

The skip-concatenate algorithm, which is the main original contribution, is underspecified. The manuscript does not precisely define the generation schedule, skip frequency, context composition, chunk overlap, treatment of sequence ends, or how the two separated context chunks are represented. Figure 5 conveys the intuition but is insufficient for independent reproduction or technical scrutiny.

The new benchmark protocols are not documented rigorously enough. The numbers and lengths of evaluated videos, clip extraction for FVD, inclusion or exclusion of observed keyframes, preprocessing, and metric implementation details are absent. Table 6 mentions only 16 SNU-FILM videos, raising particular concern about the reliability of FVD—the paper's strongest metric—without sample counts, uncertainty estimates, or sensitivity analysis.

The broad state-of-the-art and superior-quality language is stronger than the evidence. On X4K-16x, BiM-VFI is better on three of four reported metrics: LPIPS 0.055 versus 0.071, VFIPS -69.98 versus -64.80, and FloLPIPS 0.065 versus 0.082. On SNU-FILM-4x, LDF-VFI is also behind EDEN and RIFE in LPIPS. No human study, PSNR/SSIM results, or evaluation on established frame-centric protocols is provided to support the argument that these metric trade-offs correspond to better perceptual quality.

The baseline coverage is incomplete for establishing the paradigm-level claim. Methods discussed as relevant, including SGM-VFI, VFIMamba, VIDIM, LDMVFI, and other diffusion VFI systems, are not evaluated or their exclusion justified. Comparing a WAN2.1-initialized model trained on LAVIB mainly against substantially different systems also requires model-size, FLOP, memory, training-data, and training-compute reporting.

Several generalization claims exceed the experiments. Arbitrary/non-integer temporal ratios are claimed, but only integer 4x, 8x, and 16x results are shown. Arbitrary spatial resolution is represented only by one 4K benchmark. The full-versus-sparse attention study uses partially trained 6K-step models and supplies no memory measurements, so it does not isolate why full attention performs dramatically worse at 4K.

Reproducibility is currently weak: the abstract's code URL is blank, the WAN2.1 variant and parameter count are unspecified, attention-window and AR-sampling details are missing, and the runtime description is internally inconsistent—Table 4 calls runtime single-H100 performance while X4K entries use four H100 GPUs. These omissions materially affect verification of both accuracy and efficiency claims.

Most components besides skip-concatenate sampling are adaptations of established techniques: diffusion forcing, tiled VAE processing, local attention, ControlNet-style feature injection, and nearest-neighbor conditioning. This is a potentially useful integration, but because the novel sampling mechanism lacks decisive long-horizon evidence, the current scientific support does not yet outweigh the moderate originality.

strengths: The video-centric formulation is well motivated: jointly synthesizing temporal chunks can exploit dependencies that pairwise interpolation methods ignore, and the skip-concatenate ordering is an interesting task-specific approach to autoregressive drift.
The method combines diffusion forcing, spatially local/temporally dense attention, tiled VAE processing, and conditional decoding into a coherent system capable of 4K inference.

LDF-VFI obtains the best reported FVD in every evaluated setting, with especially large gains at 8× and 16× interpolation. The component studies also show meaningful FVD improvements from skip-concatenate sampling and the conditional VAE.
The paper is generally readable, and its architecture, training configuration, computational cost, and principal components are described more clearly than is typical for a system of this scale.
weaknesses: The central claim—temporally stable generation for arbitrary-length videos with error bounded independently of duration—is not established. No experiment measures error or quality as sequence length grows, and no theoretical argument proves bounded accumulation. Table 3 reports aggregate FVD, while Figure 6 presents only a single example comparing skip-concatenate against independent chunks rather than the causal baseline. This is a material evidentiary gap.

The state-of-the-art claim overstates the results. The method consistently wins FVD but is not best on LPIPS, VFIPS, or FloLPIPS: for example, BiM-VFI is substantially better on all three non-FVD metrics on X4K-16×, while EDEN or RIFE often achieves better LPIPS on SNU-FILM. Thus, the evidence supports improved distribution-level temporal quality, not generally superior per-frame fidelity.

The newly constructed benchmarks are insufficiently specified. The paper omits the number and duration of evaluation videos, exact clip construction, frame ranges, preprocessing, and a public protocol. Table 6 mentions only 16 SNU-FILM test videos; if similarly few sequences underlie FVD, that distributional estimate may be highly unstable. There are no confidence intervals, repeated evaluations, or significance analyses.

Baseline coverage and fairness are limited. Several relevant multi-frame or diffusion VFI approaches discussed in the paper, including VIDIM and LDMVFI, are absent. EDEN is recursively applied beyond its native 2× setting, while LDF-VFI uses whole-video context, large-scale LAVIB training, and a pretrained Wan2.1 backbone. The study therefore does not isolate whether gains arise from the proposed holistic formulation, model scale/pretraining, or an unfavorable inference setup for pairwise baselines.

There is no human evaluation despite explicitly rejecting PSNR/SSIM on perceptual grounds. The qualitative evidence consists of a few small examples, and deterministic reconstruction measures are largely omitted. Since FVD is the sole metric on which the method uniformly leads, stronger perceptual and temporal validation is necessary.

The core skip-concatenate procedure is not specified algorithmically: the exact generation schedule, context composition, overlap, boundary handling, and behavior at different sequence lengths are unclear. Sparse-attention window connectivity and conditional-VAE injection details are also incomplete, and the promised source-code link is blank. These are substantive reproducibility problems.

Efficiency is poor and presented somewhat misleadingly. At SNU-FILM-8×, the 16-step method takes 3.36 seconds per frame versus 0.15 for BiM-VFI; at 4K it takes 16.3 seconds per frame using four H100-class GPUs versus 1.4 seconds for BiM-VFI. This weakens the practical-usefulness claim, while the text initially describes the table as a single-GPU comparison.

Claims of arbitrary/non-integer temporal ratios and arbitrary spatial resolutions receive little or no direct evaluation. Only 4×, 8×, and 16× interpolation and one 4K benchmark are reported. Overall, the promising system and FVD gains are outweighed by insufficient support for its defining long-range-stability claim, under-specified benchmarks, and incomplete comparative validation.

strengths: The manuscript presents a useful video-centric alternative to conventional pairwise VFI, combining chunk-level diffusion forcing with autoregressive generation to exploit broader temporal context. The skip-concatenate sampling scheme is intuitive and practically motivated: independently generated skip chunks reset the dependency chain, while bridging chunks restore continuity. The ablation supports its value, reducing average FVD from 22.67 for causal autoregression to 17.05, with only a small LPIPS improvement.

Results are strong on the proposed full-video protocols. LDF-VFI obtains the best reported FVD in every setting: 8.21/15.01/26.26 on SNU-FILM at 4x/8x/16x and 51.41 on X4K-16x, compared with the strongest baseline results of 9.02/21.52/38.26 and 69.83, respectively.

The system addresses an important practical combination of long temporal context and high spatial resolution. Sparse spatial attention and tiled VAE processing allow a model trained on 512x512 crops to run at 4K, while the full-versus-sparse ablation shows substantial gains in both runtime and X4K FVD.

The component analysis is reasonably comprehensive: the paper separately examines autoregressive order, conditional decoding, sparse attention, sampling steps, temporal chunk length, and nearest-neighbor conditioning. Figures are clear and the qualitative examples show plausible improvements on difficult motion.
weaknesses: The strongest long-horizon claim is insufficiently established. The paper states that skip-concatenate sampling keeps error at a constant level for videos of arbitrary length, but provides neither an error analysis nor quantitative curves against sequence length. Dataset sequence counts and durations are also not reported clearly, so the tested temporal horizon is difficult to assess.

The comparison partially conflates architecture, context, and scale. LDF-VFI uses the entire low-frame-rate sequence and a large pretrained Wan2.1 backbone, whereas the baselines are pairwise models run independently or recursively. No parameter counts, training compute, matched-backbone control, or competitive multi-frame/video model is included, limiting attribution of the gains specifically to the proposed formulation.

Claims of superior per-frame quality are overstated. LDF-VFI is not best in LPIPS: EDEN is better at SNU-FILM-4x and 8x, and BiM-VFI is better on X4K. The advantage is primarily in FVD and temporal metrics. Reporting PSNR/SSIM or keyframe fidelity alongside perceptual metrics, and preferably a human evaluation, would better establish the fidelity-versus-plausibility tradeoff.

The new benchmark protocols lack important reproducibility details, including exact clips, splits, frame counts, preprocessing, FVD sample construction, and aggregation. This matters because FVD can be sensitive to sample count and clip formation. The abstract's source-code field is also blank, and no implementation accompanies the manuscript.

Several broad generalization claims exceed the experiments. Only one 4K benchmark supports 'arbitrary spatial resolutions,' and the claimed arbitrary/non-integer temporal ratios are not evaluated. The nearest-neighbor conditioning ablation covers only 16 short test videos and measures VAE reconstruction rather than end-to-end interpolation.

The approach is substantially slower and more resource-intensive than the strongest flow baseline: at SNU-FILM-8x, the 16-step model takes 3.36 seconds per frame versus 0.15 for BiM-VFI; X4K inference uses four H100 GPUs. Thus, the efficiency contribution is scalability through bounded/local computation, not competitive wall-clock efficiency. Exact skip-concatenate schedules and conditioning contexts should also be specified more rigorously.
